text.p: Boris Yeltsin began the long road to recovery on Wednesday after a quintuple heart bypass operation, with political rivals, foreign governments and financial markets waiting to see how fast he can get better.
Surgeons including U.S. pioneer Michael DeBakey said the operation, led by Russian Renat Akchurin, was a complete success and the patient was doing fine.

Professor George Noon told Reuters by telephone: "It is not unusual to see five bypasses. The important thing is that the vessels that were diseased were all able to be bypassed and he (Yeltsin) has done very well."
Akchurin on Tuesday declined to spell out how many bypasses he had performed, saying he did not have Yeltsin's consent to reveal the exact figure.
Noon, from the Bailey Medical Centre in Houston, came to Moscow with DeBakey as a consultant to the Russian team that carried out the operation on the 65-year-old Yeltsin.

"It was very standard and everything went in a very routine manner without complications," he said. "The vessels that were diseased were bypassed and it ended up with the number five," Noon said, adding that a couple of Yeltsin's arteries had sections which were completely blocked.

However the high number of bypasses would make no difference to the speed of recovery now that the blood supply to the heart had been reestablished. "He (Yeltsin) has really responded well and is doing fine."
Noon said there were no other special areas of concern after the operation and "a routine convalescence is what we are looking for."
Yeltsin recovered consciousness by early Tuesday evening but remained on a ventilator and his doctors planned a formal meeting at 9 a.m. (0600) on Wednesday to review his progress.
Removing the ventilator and allowing his lungs to take over will be the next crucial step.

Moscow's political elite will be watching closely to see when he is well enough to take back powers he handed over early on Tuesday to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin, including control of Russia's nuclear deterrent.

Officials indicated before the operation that this would take place with a day or two. Any delay would raise fears that Yeltsin's recovery will be more prolonged than the six to eight weeks which surgeons say is normal.
A setback for Yeltsin would also affect the price of Russian debt and Russian stocks, which have already moved up on the early news that surgery was successful.

Both the president's friends and foes in Russian politics will plan their strategies according to whether Yeltsin bounces back vigorously and takes full charge in the Kremlin, or remains the part-time president he has been for most of the last 18 months.

Foreign governments also want to know if Yeltsin will serve out the four-year term to which he was elected in July, or if he will remain a figurehead while his aides and subordinates fight over his legacy.
German Chancellor Helmut Kohl has publicly promised that no decisions will be taken on NATO expansion -- a neuralgic issue for Russia -- until Yeltsin is recovered.
"President Yeltsin will be able to return to his office and carry out his duties in normal fashion," DeBakey told reporters.

But Akchurin voiced a note of caution: "Now the very important stage of post-operative treatment is starting." Akchurin said it may be nearly a week before doctors can estimate how quickly and fully he will recover.
But if all goes well Yeltsin could leave the Cardiology Research Centre in 10 days or so, probably returning to the Barvikha sanatorium where he spent several weeks preparing for the operation.
Kremlin spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had invitations to convalesce in Germany and in Slovakia and would decide in due course with his doctors whether to accept.
For a Russian leader to convalesce abroad would mark a sharp departure from Kremlin tradition. But doctors might favour the idea if it prevented Yeltsin from returning to work too soon.
